title: Triples Whose Sum Splits Evenly
statement:
You get an array nums and a positive integer d. Count the triples of positions i < j < k such that nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] is divisible by d.

Triples are counted by position, so equal values at different positions form different triples.

examples.why: Every choice of 3 positions out of 4 works, and there are 4 of them.

hints: Only remainders mod d matter. If you fix two of the three numbers, what remainder must the third have?
Fix the middle index j and the right index k. The left value must have remainder (−(nums[j] + nums[k])) mod d. How fast can you count such values to the left of j?

Keep a hash map of remainders seen strictly before j. Loop j from left to right, loop k over everything after j and add the map's count for the needed remainder; then add nums[j]'s remainder to the map.

explain.intuition:
This is three-sum with a remainder instead of an exact target. Pin down two of the three positions and the third is forced up to its remainder: it must be (−(nums[j] + nums[k])) mod d. Instead of searching for it, ask a hash map how many earlier values have that remainder.

The order of the loops keeps every triple counted exactly once. The map holds only positions before j, and k runs only after j, so each triple is counted at its middle index and nowhere else.
steps: Create an empty map seen from remainder to count.
For each j from left to right: for each k > j, compute need = (d − (nums[j] + nums[k]) % d) % d and add seen[need] to the answer.
pitfalls: Forgetting the outer % d in need, so a sum already divisible by d looks for remainder d instead of 0.
Adding nums[j] to the map before the inner loop, which lets i equal j.
Counting by remainder groups and treating repeated groups like distinct ones: three values from the same group give C(c, 3) triples, not c³.

solutions.title: Check every triple
solutions.idea: Three nested loops over i < j < k.

solutions.title: Fix the middle, look up the left
solutions.idea: For each middle j and right k the left remainder is forced. A map of remainders seen before j answers how many lefts fit.

followups: d is small (say at most 100). Count triples in O(n + d²) using only the counts of each remainder.
Count quadruples instead. Which pairing of loops keeps it at O(n²)?
